**Text A: A letter to parents**

*This letter was sent to parents by the head of a (fictional) secondary school in Bulawayo.*

Dear Parents and Guardians,

From the start of next term, I propose that mobile phones be banned at Mopani Park High School during the school day. Students who bring a phone will hand it in at the office when they arrive and collect it at four o'clock.

I do not make this proposal lightly. Over the past year, teachers have told me again and again that lessons are interrupted by buzzing phones and that students check messages under their desks instead of listening. Concentration suffers, and so do results.

There is a more serious problem. Last term the school dealt with several cases in which photographs of students were taken and shared without their permission, causing real distress. Phones in school make this kind of bullying easy and instant.

I am also saddened by what I see at break. Where students once played football or sat talking in groups, many now sit side by side in silence, each staring at a screen. School should be a place where young people learn to get on with one another face to face.

Finally, phones are expensive. Every month we deal with disputes about phones that have been lost, broken or stolen, which takes up time that teachers should spend teaching.

I know that some parents worry about being unable to contact their children. The school office telephone is staffed throughout the day, and any urgent message will be passed on at once. Others say phones help with learning; our computer room provides internet access under supervision.

I invite you to share your views at the parents' meeting at the end of the month.

Yours faithfully,

Mrs P. Chinembiri, Head

**Text B: Don't ban it, teach it**

*This post appeared on the student blog of the same school. It was written by Kudakwashe, a Form 5 student.*

Our head wants to ban phones. I understand why, but I think a ban is the wrong answer.

First, a ban punishes everybody for the behaviour of a few. Most of us do not text in lessons or share cruel photographs. Why should we lose a useful tool because some students misuse it?

And phones are useful. I use mine as a dictionary, a calculator and a place to record homework. When the board is full, I photograph the notes instead of copying them out while the teacher waits. The head mentions the computer room, but there are twenty computers for nine hundred students, and it is almost always booked. Some teachers already use phones well: our Geography teacher asks us to look up live weather maps in lessons, and our Shona teacher records our oral practice so that we can hear our own mistakes.

Many of us travel long distances by kombi. If a kombi breaks down or we are delayed, our parents want to hear from us directly, not from an office that closes at half past four. Handing in nine hundred phones each morning would also mean long queues, and who would pay if one were damaged?

Cyberbullying is real, but it does not stop at the school gate. Most of it happens in the evening, on the same phones. Banning phones at school will not stop it; teaching students to respect each other online might.

We will all use phones for the rest of our lives. School is where we should learn to use them sensibly, not where we pretend they do not exist. I suggest clear rules: phones switched off in lessons unless a teacher asks for them, a phone-free area at break, serious consequences for misuse, and lessons on staying safe online.

**Question 1**

**(a)** Evaluate the arguments for and against the proposed phone ban in Text A and Text B.

Identify **five** points. For each, say whether the argument is strong or weak and explain why, referring to the texts.

points.description: One mark for each valid evaluative point that identifies an argument, says whether it is strong or weak, and explains why with reference to the texts, to a maximum of 5
indicators: The head's distraction argument is fairly strong: it is based on repeated reports from teachers, though no figures are given
The cyberbullying argument is only partly convincing: Text B points out that most of it happens after school, so a ban treats a symptom, not the cause
The office-phone solution is weak for journeys home: the office closes at half past four (Text B), when students are travelling
The computer room argument is undermined by Text B's point that twenty computers serve nine hundred students
The point about lost and stolen phones backfires: collecting nine hundred phones makes the school responsible for them, as Text B suggests
The head's claim about break times is an emotional appeal based on personal impression rather than evidence
Text B's *punishes everybody for a few* is persuasive but does not answer the evidence that lessons are disrupted
Text B's rules rely on self-discipline, which the head says has already failed (students check phones secretly)
Text B's argument about learning to use technology sensibly is strong because it looks to students' future lives

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The head's distraction argument is strong because it comes from teachers' repeated experience. Her cyberbullying point is weaker: as Kudakwashe notes, most bullying happens in the evening, so a ban would not stop it. Her office-phone solution fails for the journey home, because the office closes at half past four. Her computer-room argument collapses if twenty machines serve nine hundred students. However, Kudakwashe's proposed rules depend on self-control that, according to the head, students have not shown.

parts.explanation: Evaluation means judging: is the argument supported by evidence, does it contradict itself, does the other text answer it? A list of arguments without judgement earns little.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Good evening, Mrs Chinembiri, teachers and parents.

I want to begin by agreeing with our head about one thing: there is a problem. Phones do buzz in lessons, and some students do check messages under their desks. Worse, some have used phones to share cruel photographs. Nobody in this hall should defend that.

But is a complete ban the answer? I don't believe it is.

Think about what a ban would really mean. Every morning, nine hundred phones would be queued, collected and stored, and the school would become responsible for every one that was cracked or lost, the very disputes Mrs Chinembiri hopes to end. And what about the journey home? Many of us ride kombis for an hour or more. If one breaks down at six o'clock, the office is closed. Parents, would you not want to hear from your child directly?

We are told the computer room can replace our phones for learning. With twenty computers shared among nine hundred students, that is simply not realistic. My phone is my dictionary, my calculator and my homework diary.

As for cyberbullying, most of it happens in the evening, far from school. A ban would move it out of sight; it would not end it. Only teaching respect online can do that.

So I propose something different: a term-long trial of strict rules. Phones switched off and in bags during lessons unless a teacher asks for them. A phone-free area at break, so that football and conversation return. Confiscation for a week for anyone who breaks the rules, and expulsion-level seriousness for sharing images without consent. And regular lessons on staying safe online.

If, at the end of the term, the rules have failed, I will accept the ban. But please give us the chance to prove that we can use phones responsibly. After all, isn't that what school is meant to teach us?

Thank you.

**Text A: A brighter future for Mutendere**

*This article was published in a local newspaper by the company that wants to build a shopping centre in the (fictional) town of Mutendere.*

Mutendere deserves better than a two-hour round trip every time a family needs new school shoes. That is why Greenstone Properties is proud to propose Vlei View, a modern shopping centre on the open land at Tsuro Vlei, just five minutes from the town centre.

Vlei View will bring eighty shops, a supermarket, a pharmacy, a cinema and a food court under one roof, with safe, well-lit parking for four hundred cars. For the first time, residents will be able to shop, bank and relax close to home, saving money on transport and time on the road.

The project will create jobs: we estimate several hundred during construction and many more when the shops open. Local builders, suppliers and young people looking for their first job will all benefit. The rates paid by the centre will give the town council money to repair roads and improve services for everyone.

Vlei View will also give Mutendere something it has never had: a place where families can spend a Saturday together. The food court and cinema will offer young people somewhere safe and supervised to meet, instead of hanging around the bus terminus with nothing to do. Local craftspeople will be offered stalls in the central courtyard at reduced rents for the first year.

We know that some residents value the vlei. We share their concern for nature. That is why the plans include a landscaped eco-park with ponds, walking paths and indigenous trees, open to the public free of charge. Our engineers have designed modern drainage to carry rainwater safely away from the site.

At the moment, Tsuro Vlei is empty land that produces nothing but mosquitoes. Vlei View will turn it into the heart of a growing town. Mutendere's future is ready to be built. Let's build it together.

**Text B: A letter to the editor**

*This letter was written in reply by Mrs Agnes Mazvita, a retired science teacher and member of the Friends of Tsuro Vlei.*

Sir,

Greenstone Properties calls Tsuro Vlei "empty land". Anyone who has walked there knows it is nothing of the kind.

A vlei is a sponge. In the rainy season it soaks up water and releases it slowly, keeping the river flowing and the boreholes of the eastern suburbs full long into the dry season. Cover it with concrete and car parks, and the rain will rush off the hard surfaces instead. The low-lying houses of Mutendere East, which already flood in a heavy storm, will flood more often. "Modern drainage" carries water away; it does not store it.

The vlei is also alive. Crowned cranes feed there every year, and our primary schools take children on nature walks to see them. A few decorative ponds in an eco-park cannot replace a whole wetland. A strip of grass between a car park and a busy road is not a place where cranes will land, or where children will learn anything about wetlands.

The company talks about jobs, but says nothing about the jobs that would be lost. Dozens of families grow vegetables on the edge of the vlei and sell them in the market. Many of the small shopkeepers in the town centre could also lose their customers to the new chain stores. And construction jobs, however welcome, last only until the building is finished.

Nobody is against progress. Mutendere does need better shops. But the old brickworks on the Harare road has stood empty for ten years and is just as close to town. Build there, and we can have new shops and keep our vlei.

Yours faithfully,

Agnes Mazvita

Dear Councillors,

**Proposed Vlei View shopping centre at Tsuro Vlei**

I am writing as a resident of Mutendere to urge the council to refuse permission for the shopping centre on Tsuro Vlei, while encouraging Greenstone Properties to build on a more suitable site.

Let me be clear: Mutendere needs better shops. A two-hour round trip for school shoes is costly and tiring, and a supermarket, pharmacy and safe parking close to home would benefit every family. On this point, the developer is right.

However, the choice of site is badly mistaken. Greenstone describes the vlei as 'empty land that produces nothing but mosquitoes'. That is simply untrue. As Mrs Mazvita explains, the vlei acts like a sponge, storing rainwater and keeping our river and boreholes supplied into the dry season. Concrete would send that water rushing into Mutendere East, which already floods. The company's 'modern drainage' would carry the water away faster; it would not store it. Nor can a few ornamental ponds replace a wetland where crowned cranes feed and our children learn about nature.

The promise of jobs also deserves scrutiny. The company offers only an estimate, and most construction jobs end when the building is finished. Meanwhile, the families who grow vegetables beside the vlei, and many small shopkeepers in the town centre, could lose their income. The council must count the jobs lost as well as those gained.

There is a better way. The old brickworks on the Harare road has stood empty for ten years and is equally close to town. A centre there would bring the same shops, the same rates for our roads, and fewer risks.

I therefore ask the council to reject the current application and to invite Greenstone Properties to submit plans for the brickworks site instead. In this way Mutendere can have both progress and its vlei.

Yours faithfully,

T. Ncube

**Weekend tutoring: help or harm?**

*A family magazine asked two people for their views on the growing number of secondary students who attend paid lessons at weekends. Both are fictional.*

**Text A: Mr Tafadzwa Gumbo, father of a Form 4 student**

My daughter goes to extra lessons every Saturday morning and on Sunday afternoons, and it is the best money I have ever spent.

Let us be honest about our schools. Her class has more than fifty students. However hard the teachers work, and many work very hard, they cannot explain a difficult topic five different ways until every child understands. At her tutor's house there are eight students around a table. If she is lost, she can say so, and someone will help her.

Competition is fierce. Places in the best A Level schools go to students with the best results, and I want my daughter to have every chance. Her tutor has taught for many years and knows exactly how examiners think: how to set out an answer, how to manage time, which mistakes cost marks. That knowledge is not in any textbook.

The results speak for themselves. Last year her mathematics mark was disappointing. This term, after six months of extra lessons, it has risen by a whole grade, and she is far more confident.

There is another benefit that people forget. Teenagers with empty weekends find ways to fill them, and not always good ways. My daughter's weekends are organised, she has a quiet place to study with serious friends, and I know where she is.

Some people say tutoring is unfair to families who cannot pay. I understand that, but I cannot hold my own daughter back to make the system fairer. Every parent does what they can for their children. For us, that means sacrifices elsewhere: we rarely eat out, and her school shoes will have to last another year.

**Text B: Mrs Ruth Dube, a school counsellor**

Every week I meet students who are exhausted. They are in class from seven until four, do homework until late, then spend Saturday and Sunday in more lessons. When do they rest? When do they help at home, go to church, play sport or simply sit with their families? One Form 4 boy told me recently that he had not had a free afternoon since January.

Young people need time to recover, just as athletes do. Students who never stop are not necessarily learning more; often they are too tired to learn anything well. I see more and more anxiety among students who feel that whatever they do is never enough.

Some tutors are excellent. Others have no teaching qualification at all and simply drill students on old exam questions without helping them to understand. Parents rarely know which kind they are paying for.

I also worry about fairness. Families who can pay buy an advantage; families who cannot are left behind, however talented their children are. And some students start to pay less attention in school, thinking, "My tutor will explain it on Saturday." Others stop asking questions in class altogether. Why risk looking foolish in front of fifty classmates when you can ask a tutor in private? Yet learning to ask questions in public, and discovering that being wrong is part of learning, is a skill every young person needs.

There are better answers. Schools can run free homework clubs after lessons. Students can form study groups and teach each other, which is one of the best ways to learn. Parents can make sure their children have a quiet place to work, enough sleep and at least one free day a week.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Weekend tutoring: is it worth it?**

It's Saturday morning. While some of us are still asleep, hundreds of students are already sitting at a tutor's kitchen table with a past paper. Are they the smart ones, or are they running on empty?

Parents like Mr Gumbo make a strong case. When a class has more than fifty students, even the most dedicated teacher cannot re-explain a topic until everyone understands. Around a table of eight, you can admit you are lost. A good tutor can also teach exam technique: how to set out an answer and use your time. With A Level places so competitive, it is easy to see why parents pay.

But look closely at the evidence. Mr Gumbo's proof is his own daughter's improved grade. That is good news for her, but one example cannot tell us whether tutoring works for everyone, or whether she would have improved anyway.

Mrs Dube, a counsellor who sees many students, raises worries that are harder to dismiss. Students who work seven days a week are often too exhausted to learn well, and anxiety is rising. Not every tutor is qualified, and some simply drill old questions. And what about fairness? Talent should not depend on what your parents can afford.

So what should we do? Tutoring is not the enemy, but it is not magic either. If you need help with one subject, a single, well-chosen session a week can make a real difference, provided you check that the tutor actually explains rather than drills. But protect at least one completely free day for rest, family and fun. Your brain needs it.

And our school could help everyone, not just those who can pay. Free homework clubs and student-led study groups cost nothing and teach us to teach each other.

The best results come not from the most hours, but from the best-rested, best-supported students.

**Text A: Bring our school into the twenty-first century**

*This statement was written by Mr Phiri, the computer studies teacher at Chengetai Secondary School (a fictional school), for a meeting about how to spend the money raised by the school's sponsored walk.*

The sponsored walk raised more money than anyone expected, and we have a once-in-a-generation chance to spend it well. I believe we should build a computer laboratory.

Our students will leave school into a world that runs on technology. Banks, hospitals, farms and offices all need people who can type, use spreadsheets and find information online. Employers expect these skills, and colleges assume them. Yet in a survey of our own Form 3 and 4 students last month, three out of four said they had never used a desktop computer, and most have no computer at home. If school does not teach these skills, nobody will.

Computers also open a door to knowledge. With an internet connection, a student in our school can read the latest science, watch lessons from expert teachers and research any topic in minutes. Coursework can be typed, saved and improved instead of copied out again and again.

Computers help teachers too. Notes, tests and records could be prepared once and printed or shared, saving hours of copying on the board, and students who miss lessons through illness could catch up from saved material. A well-equipped laboratory would also help us attract good teachers, who increasingly expect these tools. When the walk was organised, many students told me they hoped the money would bring computers.

Our two old computers in the office are not enough. A laboratory of thirty machines would allow a whole class to learn at once, and the room could be open after school for students to complete their homework.

Some will say that computers are expensive to maintain. That is true, but so is falling behind. Our students deserve the same chances as students in town schools.

**Text B: Books first**

*This statement was written for the same meeting by Mrs Moyo, the school librarian.*

I agree that our students need computer skills. But before we spend this money, I ask the committee to visit our library. Half the shelves are broken. Many of the books are older than the teachers. We have one copy of each set book for classes of forty-five.

Reading underpins every subject. A student who reads well can learn from any textbook, follow any exam question and teach herself what she missed. A student who struggles to read will struggle everywhere, with or without a computer. Many of our students come from homes with no books at all. For them, the school library is the only place where they meet a story for pleasure, and students who enjoy reading tend to read more, and more widely.

Books also work when the electricity does not. During power cuts, which happen often, a computer laboratory is just a locked room full of silent screens. A book can be read by daylight, carried home and shared with a younger brother.

Computers bring hidden costs: internet bills, repairs, software, security grilles, and a trained person to look after them. Our sponsored walk will not happen every year, but those bills will arrive every month. Books, once bought, last for years.

The library is also the only quiet place in the school where students can sit and study. With new shelves, tables and a good collection of textbooks, set books and novels, it could serve hundreds of students every day.

I am not against computers. Perhaps in time we can have both. But a house needs foundations before it needs a roof, and reading is our foundation.

His promise of online knowledge, however, depends on electricity and internet, and Mrs Moyo's point about frequent power cuts weakens it. He also brushes aside maintenance costs with a slogan. **(b)** You are a student representative on the School Development Committee of Chengetai Secondary School. Write a **report** for the committee on how the money from the sponsored walk should be spent.

In your report you should:

Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but be careful to use your own words.

Write about **two hundred and fifty to three hundred and fifty words**.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Report to the School Development Committee: use of the sponsored walk funds**

**Purpose**
This report considers the two proposals for spending the money raised by the sponsored walk and makes a recommendation on behalf of the student body.

**The case for a computer laboratory**
Mr Phiri argues convincingly that employers and colleges now expect computer skills. Our own survey, in which three quarters of Form 3 and 4 students said they had never used a desktop computer, shows that the school is the only place many students will learn them. Online research and typed coursework would also benefit every subject.

However, the proposal has serious weaknesses. Thirty computers would need internet, repairs, software and security every month, but the walk money will not be repeated. In addition, frequent power cuts would often leave the laboratory unusable.

**The case for the library**
Mrs Moyo shows that the library is in poor condition, with broken shelves, out-of-date books and only one copy of each set book for classes of forty-five. Her argument that reading underpins every subject is persuasive, and books work without electricity, can be taken home and last for years. The library is also the only quiet study space in the school.

**Recommendation**
Both writers admit that the other's need is real. I therefore recommend a phased plan:

1. Spend most of the money now on repairing the library and buying class sets of set books and up-to-date textbooks.
2. Use the remainder to install a small number of computers inside the library, so that students can begin to build basic skills under supervision.
3. Before any larger laboratory is built, prepare a plan for its monthly running costs and for power backup.

This approach gives every student the reading foundation they need now while making a realistic start on digital skills.

parts.explanation: A report should be organised under headings, written in a formal, impersonal register, and end with clear, justified recommendations. Weighing both proposals fairly before deciding earns the evaluation marks.

explanation: Directed writing tests reading and writing together. Part (a) asks you to evaluate the arguments in the texts. Part (b) rewards using and evaluating a range of ideas from both texts (10 reading marks) and writing that suits the audience, is well structured and accurate (25 writing marks).
hints: Read both texts and list the arguments on each side; mark any that are weak (emotional, one-sided, unsupported or contradicted by the other text).
In part (b), do not just repeat the ideas: weigh them, challenge them and reach your own clear view.
Keep your audience in mind all the way through: the form, the register and the persuasive techniques must suit them.
